passages.V1:
Once, the world’s richest men competed over yachts, jets and private islands. Now, their status symbol is enormous GPU clusters. Elon Musk says he has 100,000 GPUs and plans to buy 200,000 more, while Mark Zuckerberg is aiming for 350,000. Yet this quest for ever-bigger computing setups cannot go on forever. Each new chip not only adds processing power but also increases the burden of keeping everything synchronised. The more GPUs there are, the more time they waste shuttling data around rather than doing useful work. Instead, computer scientists are looking for cleverer ways to train new AI models without always resorting to these colossal installations. One idea is to abandon giant bespoke clusters, with all their upfront costs, and instead distribute the task of training across multiple smaller data centres. Some researchers see this as a step towards an even bolder goal: training AI without any dedicated hardware at all.

Training a modern AI system usually involves feeding it data (text) with some sections hidden; the model then guesses what is missing. If it is wrong, it gets tweaked via backpropagation to inch closer to the correct answer next time. Running these calculations on thousands of GPUs in parallel sounds efficient, but there is a catch: constant “checkpointing,” where every chip shares updates with the others, can devour half the total training time. This inefficiency led Arthur Douillard, an engineer at Google DeepMind, to propose “Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models,” or DiLoCo. Rather than forcing 100,000 GPUs to talk to each other at every step, DiLoCo breaks them into “islands”—each a self-contained data centre. Within an island, checkpointing proceeds as usual. Between islands, however, communications plummet, reducing that bottleneck five hundredfold.

Models trained this way may be slightly less fine-tuned for tasks they were explicitly trained on, but they often generalise better when confronted with new problems. Freed from incessant synchronisation, each “island” explores the training data in its own way before being pulled back in line. Vincent Weisser, founder of the open-source AI lab Prime Intellect, seized on DiLoCo to train Intellect-1, a 10bn-parameter model comparable to Meta’s Llama 2. His team used 30 smaller GPU clusters in eight cities across three continents. Instead of checkpointing on every training step, they did it every 500 steps and “quantised” the shared updates, throwing away the least significant data. That meant the GPUs worked productively most of the time—even when scattered across the globe. For labs that already have vast data centres, switching to distributed training may not be urgent. Yet Douillard believes this approach will catch on, given how much it cuts costs and complexity. For smaller outfits, the benefits are immediate, since vast GPU farms are rare and expensive. The dream of fully decentralised AI goes further still: eventually tapping into billions of consumer devices, if the tricky engineering can be mastered. Models might even improve, learning from more diverse data with fewer synchronisation demands. Then the billionaires may have to find something else to measure.
passages.V2:
In 2008, archaeologists discovered a large cemetery in southwest England. Located near the village of Winterborne Kingston in Dorset, the burial ground contained human remains dating back to Britain’s Iron Age, which lasted from around 800 B.C.E. to 43 C.E. The bodies belonged to a Celtic tribe known as the Durotriges. Since intact remains from this period are rare, the researchers were happy to have discovered the cemetery in the first place. But when they began to sequence DNA from dozens of bodies buried at the site, they were in for an even bigger surprise. The DNA analysis showed that many of the individuals in this community shared the same mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which gets passed down from mothers to children. They were related through the female line.

This indicates that the group was what’s known as a “matrilocality,” in which newly married men left their families to join their bride’s community. Matrilocalities are relatively rare in prehistoric Europe: After marriage, women typically left their community to join their new husband’s village in an arrangement known as a “patrilocality.” The Durotriges who lived in southwest England are thought to be among the first recorded matrilocal systems in European prehistory. In total, the team studied the genomes of 57 individuals buried at the site between 100 B.C.E to 100 C.E. Many of the Durotriges could be traced back to the same shared female ancestor, including an adult woman, her daughter, her granddaughters and potentially her great-grandson. Most of the individuals who did not share the same matrilineal DNA were male, which suggests they married into the group. “My jaw dropped,” says lead author Lara Cassidy, a geneticist at Trinity College Dublin. “This was a clear signature of matrilocality, or husbands moving to live with their wives’ families—a pattern we’d never seen before in prehistoric Europe.”

Armed with these results, the researchers began to look for other traces of matrilocality across prehistoric Britain. They investigated human remains from more than 150 archaeological sites covering a period of roughly 6,000 years—and found several other examples of matrilocal communities in Britain. It’s still not clear exactly how prevalent matrilocal communities were in Iron Age Britain, but future studies might help answer that question. Additional research might also take a closer look at the unrelated men buried at the site, investigating where they grew up and how far they traveled to join their wives. Women living in matrilocal communities likely had more influence than women living in patrilocalities. They also had the benefit of staying with their families and support networks. But even in matrilocalities, men still typically held positions of power.

“They tend to be the village chief more often, but they might not get elected without the help of their daughters, sisters and wives, who have soft power and a lot of influence,” Cassidy says. “[Women] aren’t just confined to the domestic sphere.” After the Romans invaded Britain during the first century C.E., they wrote about British women with high levels of power and multiple husbands. But scholars are divided as to whether the Romans actually observed these women or were merely spinning cautionary tales.
passages.V3:
MANAGERS ARE better equipped than ever to make good decisions. They are more aware that human judgment is fallible. They have oodles of data about customers and products. They can use artificial intelligence to analyse and synthesise information with unprecedented speed. But as the pendulum swings inexorably away from gut instinct towards data-based decisions, firms need to be alive to a different set of dangers.

In a recent paper, Linda Chang of the Toyota Research Institute and co-authors identify a cognitive bias they call “quantification fixation”. The risk of relying solely on data is familiar—sometimes referred to as the McNamara fallacy, after the American secretary of defence who used misleading quantitative measures in the Vietnam war. But Ms Chang and her co-authors explain why people put disproportionate weight on numbers. Data are particularly suited for making comparisons. In one experiment, participants were asked to imagine choosing between two software engineers for a promotion. One was more likely to climb the ladder but less likely to stay; the other had a higher chance of retention but a lower probability of advancement. When only promotion likelihood was given a numerical value, participants tended to prioritize it in their decision; however, when retention was also quantified, it began to outweigh promotion in importance, influencing participants to choose the more loyal candidate.. One answer is to quantify everything. But, as the authors point out, some things are mushier. A firm’s culture is harder to express as a number than its salary levels. Data can reveal more about a startup’s financials than a founder’s resilience. Numbers allow for easy comparisons, but do not always tell the whole story.

There are other risks. Humans bring the same cognitive biases to their analysis of numbers as to other decisions. Take confirmation bias: in another experiment, undergraduates stated their expectation for a correlation between wealth and happiness before seeing a fictitious dataset. Faced with the identical graph, those who expected a positive correlation were likelier to see one. Beliefs influenced interpretation. Plenty of people struggle with basic data literacy: they often avoid competitions with larger numbers of contestants, even when the odds are the same. In a world giddy over AI models, relying on algorithms may seem sensible. In one experiment, Hossein Nikpayam and colleagues found that managers blamed decision-makers who ignored machine-led recommendations if outcomes were bad, yet gave no credit when they were good. People once said nobody got fired for buying IBM; soon, “nobody gets fired for following the algorithm” may be the modern equivalent. But there are times when humans have an advantage: datasets reflect the world as it is, not how it might be. It’s harder to evaluate radically new ideas by looking at existing patterns. Early HBO executives used instinct and contrarianism to commission shows that broke the mould—profane comedy specials, a prison drama that killed a main character in the first episode. Other networks turned down a violent mobster in therapy; HBO did not. Relying on data might have led to safer decisions.

None of this is to say that instinct trumps data, or that humans make better decisions than machines. Far from it. But it is a warning. Numbers promise rigour, certainty and objectivity. They have flaws, too.

Researcher Emily Yeh from the University of Colorado Boulder uses “Shangrilazation” to describe how Tibet’s culture and landscape have been commodified for Chinese needs. Inspired by the Shangri-La tourism zone in northern Yunnan, it references a Tibetan border region renamed after the 1933 novel Lost Horizon, which idealized Tibet as a timeless utopia. Over the last decade, Shangri-La City morphed from a neglected provincial town called Gyalthang into a tourist paradise. After the original center burned in 2014, a faux old town was built with cobblestone alleys, ancient-looking stupas, and statues of Tibetans in “traditional” poses. Millions now flock here. A bus stop proclaims Xi Jinping’s slogan: “Clear waters and green mountains are mountains of gold and silver.”

This model spread across Tibet, turning the region into a theme park for China. Grazing grounds became “nature reserves,” displacing herders. New highways draw Chinese motorists to scenic towns and renovated monasteries, while faux nomad camps serve as photo ops. For China’s stressed urbanites, Tibet promises unspoiled nature and a slower pace—where friendly locals share their land and wisdom. Nearly all tourists are Chinese, as foreign entry is restricted. In the reconstructed old town of Shangri-La, I met Jing Zheng from Hangzhou, learning thangka painting in glitter and Tibetan robes. “Sometimes, I just want to be someone else,” she said. “Today I am Drolma—a Tibetan girl free of care.” Many Han expect Tibetan Buddhism to fill the spiritual vacuum left by fading Communist ideology. In Daocheng, once an isolated village, Xiao Liu from Shenzhen arrived for a “spiritual recharge.” Work stress drove him to visit monks for clarity. “Tibetan people are so pure,” he said.

Beijing’s immense tourism investments mask a deeper political agenda. Officially, China pledges to protect Tibet’s heritage, but in practice Tibetan land, language, and culture face erasure. Nomads are resettled, Tibetan children attend Chinese boarding schools, monasteries teach “Sinicized Buddhism,” and cultural advocates risk arrest. In Lhasa, Tibetans without local residency need a special permit to enter the city, and checkpoints frequently scan IDs for weapons or flammable materials. A state-sponsored musical about Princess Wencheng—promoted as Lhasa’s must-see—claims she introduced civilization to Tibet, legitimizing Beijing’s rule. History is revised to assert Tibet has always belonged to China.

Despite harsh surveillance, protests persist. Since 2009, 159 Tibetans have self-immolated. In 2022, pop star Tsewang Norbu set himself on fire near the Potala Palace, crying “Free Tibet!” Official planning documents say tourism must advance “Xi Jinping Thought” and promote “ethnic unity.” Authorities push the idea that Tibetans are grateful members of a unified Chinese nation with a shared future. Tourism is meant to “stabilize Tibet” by steering locals away from traditional livelihoods. Some benefit from the boom, but many resent the intrusion. A Litang waitress pointed at tourists in gaudy Tibetan costumes. “So ugly,” she whispered.

16.q:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Philosophers examine the nature of laws for four main reasons. First, laws seem central to scientific practice. Second, they are pivotal to philosophical issues involving counterfactuals, explanation, and the distinction between laws and non-laws, as sparked by thinkers like Chisholm, Goodman, Hempel, and Oppenheim. Third, Goodman famously suggested a link between lawhood and inductive confirmability, prompting further interest in the problem of induction. Finally, philosophers relish a good puzzle: while “everyone here is seated” may be a true generalization, it appears too accidental to count as a law, unlike Einstein’s principle that signals cannot exceed the speed of light, which is also true but non-accidental.

21.q:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Liberal nationalists see liberal-democratic principles and pro-national attitudes as complementary. Yael Tamir, a major proponent, introduced the debate in the early 1990s and later described the nation-state as an ideal meeting point between the two. She acknowledges that either the meaningfulness of a community or its openness must be somewhat sacrificed, though different thinkers strike different balances. Her version of liberal nationalism is akin to social liberalism, aligning with those who support “solidaristic communities.” They argue that national identity fosters solidarity, which in turn supports social justice by creating stronger social bonds and mutual responsibilities. This approach shares similarities with others who contend that a sense of shared identity can strengthen democratic values and encourage a more equitable society.

Evolutionary game theory began as an application of mathematical game theory to biology, recognizing that frequency-dependent fitness introduces a strategic aspect to evolution. It has since drawn growing interest from social scientists, motivated by three factors. First, “evolution” here can be cultural, describing changes in beliefs and norms. Second, its rationality assumptions often suit social systems more accurately than those used in traditional game theory. Third, as an explicitly dynamic theory, evolutionary game theory fills a gap in the static framework of classical game theory. Consequently, it provides valuable tools for exploring how strategic behavior evolves across diverse contexts.

Universal humanists argue that banning great works of art associated with an enemy country narrows perspectives and fosters provincialism.

Cultural chauvinism, though typically criticized, can become a crucial tool of resistance in specific contexts, as exemplified by Ukraine’s stance toward Russian cultural dominance.

Advocates of universal humanism believe that art transcends politics and should remain accessible even in times of conflict.
